en: I fled here from Talas.
In a world that brought me hardship,
Cutting his twig,
Performing his rite,
The son born of my own body
I gave to Ismail.
My darling camel-calf, left by the noble one,
Has not yet learned to put on his shirt.
That I, the mad, bewildered woman,
Am his mother, he does not yet know.
His thoughts are elsewhere:
Semetey is another Sart's son.
He will seize me on my road, alas,
And despite my pleas will spare me nothing.
My sorrow-laden life
He will slaughter as a sacrifice, alas!
My thick, girth-like hair down my back
I am to braid, alas.
Wild with racing horses,
By the orphan left by my khan
I am to die, alas!
The decree ordained by God
I am to witness, alas.
My own morning star has turned against me;
I am to die, alas!
I could not escape, O God,
The sorrow and care within my heart.
Crazed with racing horses,
How shall I escape
The child born from my breast?!
Though I wail from morning till night,
My wretched life cannot escape the written decree.
Who can flee and escape,
When the time to collect their debt arrives,
From these eighteen thousand worlds?
The dug grave will take them in,
The black earth will enclose them.'
Unable to keep her courage firm,
'Well, if my death has come, I shall die.
The line that God has drawn
Has reached my head; I shall face it!
Not only I—all sorts of peoples have passed,
The holy elders have all passed.
Not only I—so many warriors have passed,
All sorts of lions have passed,
Twelve ages have passed together,
Many saints have passed.
I have no strength to leap away,
No means to turn my thoughts aside.
To say, "Oh, sister-in-law, do not weep,"
To speak words of counsel,
My dear people are not here.'
Saying so, she girded herself
And took courage now.
For death and torment,
Your mother now girded herself.
Back when her fierce champion died,
When your sister-in-law met disaster,
When Abyke, Kobosh, the six villains,
The vast wealth left by the blood-shedder
Divided into equal shares for all,
When your mourning sister-in-law Kanykei
Suffered terrible torment,
The ten treasuries of riches
Abyke, Kobosh, two villains,
Chiybyt, Kochkor, four villains,
Adybai, Kolbai, six villains,
Divided into equal shares for all.
Left to face it alone,
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykei,
Bereft of her blood-shedding hero,
At thirty-two years of age,
When King Manas died,
When your sister-in-law met calamity,
All the treasure, the countless riches—
The forty companions left by Manas
Swarmed in to look upon them.
When they turned their steeds toward her,
The woman sitting widowed
They struck and beat till she writhed.
When they devised their cruel scheme,
When they slashed her breast open,
Dragging her like a kok-boru carcass,
When the woman dressed in mourning
They dragged down along the Talas,
When they carried out their scheme,
The thick flesh of her thigh
The wretched, overgrown dog
Struck again and again that day.
The forty companions, fearing no ancestral spirit,
Drew their bows like rain
And shot their arrows like hail.
When your dear sister-in-law Kanykei
Suffered cruel humiliation,
The leopard-woman Kanykei,
Unable to stay weeping in sorrow,
Such humiliation as no one should see
Had she not endured?
The white saddlebag brought from the Alash—
Had your sorrowful sister-in-law not borne it?
The blaze-faced horses on the hills,
Fine steeds mixed with racehorses—
Had she no complaint to God?
Her little son upon her back,
All her own kin her enemies,
Surviving simply because she had not died,
With Abyke, Kobosh, the six villains,
And the forty companions, your sister-in-law
Fought alone.
A merciless struggle
Your noble sister-in-law Kanykei
Had she not fought?
Your champion's great telescope,
Keeping it as a memento,
In the fold of her wraparound skirt
She stitched it fast, securely hidden,
To pass it to her champion Semetey,
Weeping bitterly to the one God,
His father's telescope
She had set aside for Semetey,
Bound and stitched it up again.
In the fold of her wraparound skirt,
Your valiant mother Kanykei
Had hidden it securely for safekeeping.
The telescope she had brought,
From her skirt's fold,
Wailing and weeping piercingly,
Your champion's telescope
She now took out, sobbing,
To look for Taitoru.
She could not regain her composure.
If Taitoru fell behind,
She would die before her time.
A telescope wide-mouthed as a hoe,
A great telescope a full armspan long,
It had a handle made of gold,
A case shaped like a body amulet.
Its inside was lined with gold,
Its lens fashioned of precious stone,
Cut from ruby.
The outstanding smith Bolokbai
Had set it in the lens.
When a person gazed through it,
The sight filled the heart's desire.
It was pointed toward the foe,
Brought news of the enemy.
Your tiger's great telescope,
Gold was stretched upon its handle.
Forty unfoaled mares, a thousand young mares,
The lame smith Bolokbai
Had been paid for it.
Let me tell of the telescope.
In an autumn long gone,
In the valley of broad Talas,
Along Zhylgynduu and Ken-Kol,
In Kara-Buura and Chatkal,
When the multitude of Kyrgyz dwelt
In the valley of Kotormo,
Beside the dry plane tree,
Finding a land like Talas,
At twelve years old Manas Khan,
Finding a people like the Kyrgyz,
Had come from Altai and grown,
Become chief of a renowned people,
Made Zhylgynduu and Ken-Kol his land,
Become a fortunate, surpassing lion,
Stirred by his own valor,
Met many a Khydyr,
Caught from the herd and ridden
The swift steed Toruchaar,
Suffered torment from the Chinese,
And found his Kyrgyz kin.
His counselor, mighty Koshoi,
Was a khan of sacred power.
My uncle, whom he relied upon,
The dear land of Zheti-Suu
Had skillfully made his homeland,
The Kyrgyz of Zheti-Suu
Had patiently united into a people.
Receiving a letter from the caliph,
He was called the elder Koshoi.
While Koshoi ruled,
He was worn out by humiliation.
Konurbai's father,
The khan called Alooke, had arisen;
The mere news of him drove out men's souls.
The Muslim faithful were worn down.
Koshoi and the champions,
He beat them all, sparing none.
That handful of the Islamic faithful,
No warrior equal to him had been born;
They could not gain equal footing with him
And were sorely worn down then.
He levied tribute and his customs dues
Were being gathered then.
Upon that handful of Muslims
He laid many taxes and levies.
Alooke, who came from Beijing,
Was tormenting them then.
In the city of Samarkand,
Alooke settled there as an envoy,
He was ruling then.
In the city of Samarkand
He set up his marvels.
Among Alooke's marvels,
His tiger had bred fifteen cubs;
No person could come near.
His dragons numbered sixty.
Farther beyond them,
Set there by sorcery,
Was his sword-snouted elephant.
Born and raised in Altai,
Growing mighty among a renowned people,
Taking Talas for his homeland,
The Argyn and Kyrgyz people
He had deliberately gathered as his subjects.
Manas became a renowned warrior,
Went on foot, no horse could bear him,
Grew hardened, drinking blood,
Was himself called Manas the Leopard.
When the people moved to higher pastures,
In summer, when horses' tongues turn black,
Hearing words from the old tradition,
Alooke, who had come as an envoy,
The few Muslims
Had been trampled by this swine, he heard.
Manas, roused, could not stay still.
'I will seize and slaughter him,' he said,
'I will drink my fill of his blood.'
The khan watching the people's border,
Alooke in Samarkand—
To seize that man,
To slaughter him in sacrifice,
If he could, the Muslims
To set them free,
For Alooke in Samarkand
To stage a spectacle,
Manas had not yet come into his full might;
Khydyr had not yet settled upon Manas's head,
God had not yet granted his wish,
Azhybai and Bakai had not yet come.
That uniquely born, surpassing lion,
To the city of Samarkand
The fierce warrior went alone.
His chosen horse was Toruchaar,
Arkuron he led as his spare.
In Samarkand, Alooke
Had studied the wondrous arts too.
Three nights beforehand,
That Manas the Leopard would come,
Would bloody the mouth of his gate,
Would kill the guards,
'And seize me,' he thought—
Alooke had known.
That he would uproot his supporting pillar,
Would bring trouble upon his head,
